passage:
Devika, sit with me. Your Nani, Manjula, wasn't always the person making you tea.

At twenty I was with a boy called Dinesh. One day he said I'd been flirting with a boy at the bus queue. I hadn't; he'd only asked which bus went to the market. I told him so, calmly. He grumbled, then let it go.

Two weeks later it was a classmate's notes. Then a smile at the shop. Every time I explained, and every time a new accusation came, as if my answers were never the point.

I began to wonder if I'd done something wrong. Then I stopped and looked at the pattern instead. Nothing I said ever ended it.

I told my sister everything. That's what helped me see that the problem was not my behaviour.

qa.q: Why had Dinesh said Manjula was flirting at the bus queue?
qa.a: He accused her because a boy in the queue had spoken to her, though he had only asked which bus went to the market.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel as new accusations kept coming, and what changed?
qa.a: She began to feel confused and full of self-doubt, wondering if she had done something wrong, until she saw that nothing she said ever ended the accusations, so the problem was the pattern and not her behaviour.

qa.q: What helped Manjula see her situation more clearly?
qa.a: Telling her sister everything, because a trusted listener helped her see the pattern from outside.

qa.q: How might Dinesh have seen his own accusations at the time?
qa.a: He may have felt insecure and believed he was being watchful, without seeing that his suspicion had no end.

grounding: Shows being accused of things not done, answering calmly with facts, and recognising constant unfounded suspicion as a warning sign.

passage: Noor, you keep saying sorry for things you didn't do. Come, sit with your Irawati Aunty for a minute. When I was twenty-one, I was engaged to a man named Sameer. At first he was sweet. Then the questions started. 'Why were you late from college? Who was that on the phone? Why did you smile at the vegetable seller?' I would explain calmly, with facts. The bus was late. It was my sister. The vegetable seller is sixty. He'd believe me for a day, then accuse me of something new. I began to think maybe I was doing something wrong, maybe I was a bad person. My mother noticed I'd stopped laughing. She said, 'Ira, look at the pattern, not the latest question. Does it ever end?' It didn't. I ended the engagement. The family was upset for a year. I have never once regretted it. Suspicion that never stops isn't your guilt, beta. It's a warning.

qa.q: Who was actually on the phone, according to Irawati?
How had Irawati started to feel under the constant accusations?
qa.a: She began to doubt herself, feeling guilty and wondering if she was a bad person.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Irawati's story?
qa.a: Her mother telling her to look at the pattern, not the latest question, which led her to end the engagement.

qa.q: How did Irawati's mother see the situation?
qa.a: She noticed Irawati had stopped laughing and saw the endless suspicion as the real problem.

grounding: An elder's story of being constantly accused without cause, staying calm with facts, and recognising never-ending suspicion as a warning sign.

passage: It was the night before Swati's final practical exam, and Gopika had called four times. 'Why were you online at eleven? Who were you talking to?' 'My lab group, about the titration steps,' Swati said, steady. 'I can send you the screenshot.' 'You always have a screenshot ready. That's suspicious in itself.' Swati closed her notes. It was the third accusation this week. Last Monday it was a classmate's birthday post; on Thursday, a late bus. Each time she'd stated the facts calmly, and each time a new question arrived. She had started apologising for things she hadn't done. Sitting on the hostel floor, she did what her counsellor had suggested and listed the week's accusations. Six. None true. None ended. 'Gopika,' she said, 'I've answered every question honestly. I can't keep proving I'm innocent. I think we need to talk about this after my exam, maybe with a counsellor.' Then she switched her phone to silent and slept.

qa.q: How many accusations were on Swati's list for the week?
How did Swati feel after a week of accusations?
qa.a: She had started feeling guilty and apologising for things she hadn't done.

qa.q: What steps did Swati take to protect herself?
qa.a: Stated facts calmly, listed the accusations to see the pattern, proposed talking with a counsellor, and silenced her phone to sleep.

qa.q: What might Gopika's constant suspicion suggest?
qa.a: Gopika's own insecurity, which is a warning sign rather than proof of Swati's guilt.

grounding: Shows a young woman repeatedly accused without cause, staying calm with facts and recognising unending suspicion as a warning sign.
